name: Goodnotes
tagline: Handwritten note-taking and PDF annotation for iPad and Apple Pencil, with searchable ink and shared notebooks.

pricing.basis: annual subscription, with a one-time lifetime option on some platforms
pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The hard part of a handwriting app is ink: sub-frame latency, pressure and tilt curves, predictive stroke rendering. Apple hands most of that over for free in PencilKit, so an agent can get you a real notebook app with pages, PDF import, lasso, and local storage in a weekend. Where it falls apart is everything around the ink: multi-device sync, handwriting search across hundreds of documents, templates, shape snapping, and the thousand small gestures Goodnotes has sanded smooth over a decade. You also need a Mac, Xcode, and a way to keep the build on your iPad past the seven-day free provisioning window. Good enough if you want a personal, local, no-subscription notebook. Not good enough if your entire academic or work archive already lives in it.
coreLoopDIY: A local iPad notebook app built on PencilKit and PDFKit: create notebooks, write with Apple Pencil, import and annotate PDFs, and export pages, all stored on-device.
requirements: An iPad and an Apple Pencil for real testing, the simulator is useless for ink
An Apple ID for sideloading, and a paid developer account if you want the build to survive past seven days
Basic comfort with Swift and SwiftUI when the agent's first build does not compile
whatYouLose: Cross-device sync, your notes live on one iPad unless you wire up CloudKit yourself
Handwriting search and OCR across your whole library, which is the feature people actually depend on
Shared notebooks, collaboration, and the classroom and study-group workflows
Polished extras: templates, stickers, shape and math recognition, flashcards, audio recording tied to strokes
Any guarantee that the file format you invent on Saturday is readable in two years
moatNotes: The ink engine is partly Apple's gift, but the handwriting recognition across dozens of languages and the decade of gesture tuning are not.
whyPeopleStillPay: People pay because their notes are already in it, often years of them, and because the app does not make them think about the pen. A DIY PencilKit notebook can feel surprisingly close for an afternoon of writing, then you discover you cannot find the lecture from March, your iPhone shows nothing, and the lasso behaves oddly near page edges. For a small annual fee that is a bad trade for most people. For someone who wants a plain, offline, format-stable notebook they fully own, it is a defensible one.
notes: The ink is easy now, the library management is not.
prompt:
Build a local-first handwritten notebook app for iPad called InkBook.

Stack: Swift, SwiftUI, PencilKit, PDFKit. Target iPadOS 17 or later. Xcode project, no third-party packages, no backend, no accounts, no analytics.

Core features:
1. A library screen listing notebooks as a grid of cover thumbnails. Create, rename, duplicate, delete.
2. A notebook is an ordered list of pages. Each page stores a PKDrawing plus an optional background: blank, ruled, dotted, grid, or an imported PDF page.
3. Editor screen: PKCanvasView wrapped for SwiftUI, PKToolPicker for pen, pencil, highlighter, eraser, and lasso. Pinch to zoom, two-finger pan, Apple Pencil draws and finger scrolls by default with a toggle.
4. Page navigation: swipe or a thumbnail sidebar. Add page, insert page after current, delete page, reorder by drag.
5. Import a PDF with the document picker: render each page as a PDFPage background with its own drawing layer on top. Export the annotated notebook back out as a flattened PDF with PDFKit.
6. Persistence: one folder per notebook in the app Documents directory. Write each page drawing as PencilKit data plus a JSON manifest describing page order and backgrounds. Save on a debounce after strokes change and on backgrounding. Make the format readable and documented in README.md.
7. Autosave recovery: if the app is killed mid-edit, reopen on the same page with the last saved strokes.

Explicitly out of scope: sync across devices, collaboration, handwriting OCR or search inside ink, shape recognition, templates store, stickers, audio recording, any login.

Ship a README.md covering how to run it, how to get it onto a physical iPad, the on-disk file format, and the known limitations above. No secrets are needed, so do not create a .env file.

Write the app so it builds and runs on first try in the iPad simulator, then note in the README that ink latency and pressure only make sense on real hardware.
